To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) dispersal is an independent trait of life-history variation; 2) the evolution of dispersal is driven by the costs of movement; 3) dispersal is a central component of the evolution of spatial structure in ecological communities; 4) dispersal is central to the evolution of spatial variation in life histories; 5) dispersal is expected to be a key component in understanding how species adapt to environmental change.

(i) dispersal should be considered as a central, and independent trait in the life history of organisms and (ii) the spatial distribution of habitat patches and their temporal variability strongly affect the evolution of dispersal, and thus the spatial distribution of life histories.

(i) the inclusion of disperser as a central and independent life-history trait is likely to change our view of how life-history variation is shaped in spatially structured and heterogeneous landscapes; and (ii) this is likely to have profound implications for population spread, invasion success and coexistence in spatially heterogeneous landscapes.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the evolutionary dynamics of dispersal, the impact on population and community dynamics, and the consequences for biodiversity and conservation.
the evolution of dispersal as a central and independent axis of life history variation.
the evolution of dispersal and the consequences of its integration into life history theory.

dispersal has been neglected in life history theory, but is a central trait in ecology and evolution.

dispersal should be considered as a principal axis in life histories, independent of other major life history traits, and that the spatial configuration of the environment is a key factor determining the evolutionary trajectories of dispersal.

dispersal is a central and independent dimension of life history, that is free of constraints, and that its evolution is expected to be strongly influenced by the spatial structure of environments and the costs of movement.

dispersal is an independent axis of variation, which is central in life history and population ecology.

the evolution of dispersal is a central and independent component in life-history theory, and that its integration into the theory of life-history evolution has far reaching consequences for our understanding of the evolution of biodiversity.
dispersal is not only a trait, but also a process that is central to life history and population dynamics.

dispersal is a central trait of life histories, and that it should be treated as such.
dispersal is a key trait in life history evolution and that it should be explicitly considered as such.
